records.current_summary:
Israel is the Middle East's most progressive destination for trans visitors, with no criminalisation, anti-discrimination protections, court-based legal gender recognition (with dead-name removal from IDs as of 2025), publicly funded transition healthcare, and Tel Aviv as a regional queer hub.

Two traveler-specific risks pull the score down. First, Ben-Gurion Airport has no regulations for interacting with trans travelers — documented humiliating questioning and detainment, with surgery demanded for gender recognition ("If you don't undergo surgery, you're still a male"). Every foreign visitor transits Ben-Gurion, making this a high-probability friction point. Second, violence is rising sharply: 433 homophobic/transphobic physical incidents were reported in 2025, including dating-app traps and organized ambushes, with transgender people "bearing the brunt." Trump's anti-trans rhetoric is reportedly inflaming the local climate.

The right-wing Netanyahu coalition and the Israel-Hamas war aftermath have weakened protections, though the National Security Committee has convened on LGBTQ public-space security.

prison_adds.title: Keepin’ It “Real”: Israel’s Segregation of Transgender Prisoners and the Transgender/Cisgender Binary (Lihi Yona, Buffalo Journal of Gender, Law & Social Policy, Vol. 24, p. 43)
prison_adds.summary: Law-journal article documenting that Israel’s response to transgender prisoners’ vulnerability has been to isolate/segragate them, keeping trans inmates apart from the rest of the prison population rather than placing them in facilities matching their gender identity. Establishes that a trans prisoner faces isolation-based custody as the default management practice.

prison_adds.title: New Israel Fund – Victory for Transgender Rights in Israeli Prisons
prison_adds.summary: October 2019 precedent-setting case: an Israeli court ordered the Israel Prison Service to provide hormone-replacement therapy to a trans woman prisoner and transfer her from a male prison to a female one, after ACRI petitioned. The prisoner was initially placed in a separate wing of the women’s prison, and ACRI prepared a further petition to have her housed with the general population — showing case-by-case placement review by the courts, and that trans women have at times been held in men’s prisons in Israel.

records.current_summary:
Jamaica is dangerous for trans visitors. The Offences Against the Person Act (buggery law, up to 10 years) remains on the books and shapes police culture; there is no legal gender recognition and no anti-discrimination protection. The defining case is Dwayne Jones, a gender-nonconforming 16-year-old beaten, stabbed, and shot to death by a mob at a 2013 street party after being outed — whose killing police failed to investigate, now the subject of an Inter-American Commission case (Dwayne Jones v. Jamaica) documenting state failure to protect trans life.

Police harassment of trans women is documented in the public-health literature, and mob justice against perceived LGBT people remains a live risk — community members report that violence against trans people (beatings, stonings) is common but rarely reported because there is no point. Tourist resorts (Montego Bay, Negril, Ocho Rios) are heavily insulated bubbles where incidents are rare, but a visibly trans visitor outside them faces real outing-violence risk with indifferent police.

prison_adds.title: Gays ostracised in prison – study
prison_adds.summary: Jamaica Gleaner reporting (5 Feb 2019) on UWI lecturer Carla Moore's 2018 study (Apr-Nov 2018, funded by the Inter-American Institute of Human Rights, the IBA and the UN Latin American Institute for the Prevention of Crime): Jamaicans perceived as gay, bisexual or transgender 'are isolated' in Jamaica's penal institutions and rehabilitation opportunities for them are 'basically non-existent'. Inmates' movement inside facilities is severely curtailed and access to resources often limited because of entrenched homophobia/transphobia - other prisoners refuse to touch objects or sit on seats used by gay prisoners. The study estimated that about 300 of the 1,800 prisoners at Tower Street Adult Correctional Centre belong to sexual or gender minorities and reported that lesbians face prevalent 'corrective rape'. Evidence that LGB/trans prisoners are socially ostracised and isolated rather than integrated, with no specialised housing policy documented.

prison_adds.title: Jamaica 2023 Human Rights Report (US Department of State)
prison_adds.summary: US State Dept country report: 'Prisoner-on-prisoner violence was common, including severe violence against prisoners targeted for their perceived lesbian, gay, bisexual, transgender, queer, or intersex (LGBTQI+) identity'; correctional facilities were significantly overcrowded (Tower Street maximum-security cells at three times capacity), with harsh, life-threatening conditions, and a January 2023 video showed an inmate at a pretrial police lockup beaten and attacked with scalding liquid by inmates accusing him of being gay. The report also records that Jamaica barred legal gender registration ('Individuals were not legally allowed to register a change of gender'), that the buggery law (up to 10 years' hard labour) criminalised consensual same-sex conduct, and that no anti-discrimination law protected SOGI. Official-state confirmation that trans prisoners face identity-targeted violence in Jamaican prisons with no gender-recognition framework for accommodation decisions.

records.current_summary:
Japan is a very safe destination for transgender visitors in practice, with a legal framework that lags behind. There is no national anti-discrimination law — the 2023 "understanding" law is symbolic — and legal gender change still requires a court process. But courts have moved in trans people's favour: the Supreme Court struck down the sterilisation requirement for legal gender change in 2023 and ruled workplace bathroom restrictions on a transgender woman illegal the same year.

Day-to-day risk is minimal: violent crime is rare, visibly trans visitors report curiosity more often than hostility, hotels and transport are unproblematic, and the capital and the second city have an established queer scene. The main practical challenge is the strictly gendered, full-nudity culture of hot springs (onsen) — manageable using guides to gender-neutral or private rental baths and mixed open-air baths, which travellers actively share.

Same-sex marriage remains unavailable, which matters for a trans visitor planning to travel with a partner on spousal status. One caveat: online transphobic rhetoric and misinformation rose visibly during the 2023 legislative debates, indicating a live culture-war current, though it rarely translates into street-level trouble for visitors.

prison_adds.title: Prison warned over treatment of transgender inmate | The Asahi Shimbun
prison_adds.summary: Asahi Shimbun (9 Sep 2023): Gifu's Kasamatsu Prison — a women's prison — holds an inmate who is listed as female on her family register but identifies as a man (diagnosed with gender identity disorder). The Gifu Prefecture Bar Association demanded the prison allow him male clothes and a male hairstyle; after years with no policy change, the bar association issued a formal 'warning' to the prison in Sep 2023. The case shows Japan places convicted trans inmates in facilities matching their registered (family-register) sex rather than their gender identity, while treatment conditions inside remain contested at the prefecture level.

prison_adds.title: Japan Should End Abusive Detention Conditions for Transgender People | Human Rights Watch
prison_adds.summary: HRW (11 Jun 2025): Tomoya Asanuma, a prominent transgender activist, was arrested in March 2024, held for more than 100 days in pre-trial detention and charged with assault; he was detained among men at a pre-trial detention centre, initially denied hormone treatment (until a doctor recommended it), mocked for his transgender identity in interrogations, and only allowed to shower away from other detained men after requests. HRW frames this as part of Japan's 'hostage justice' detention abuse and the legal limbo trans people face. For the prison-housing axis, it documents that a trans man's custodial placement followed his male legal sex, with accommodations (hormones, segregated showers) granted only grudgingly.

records.current_summary:
Kyrgyzstan is dangerous for trans visitors. Same-sex conduct has been legal since 1998 and there is no expression statute, but legal gender recognition has been removed, police abuse and extortion of LGBT people are documented, and an active anti-LGBT political campaign is running in the country — in 2023-2024 two discriminatory laws targeted the LGBTI community and restricted LGBTI organisations, with homophobic and transphobic legislator rhetoric accompanying them.

For a visitor: no expression statute, but LGR removal, a police extortion culture, and the political campaign make being outed risky.

prison_adds.title: Kyrgyzstan: Events of 2024 — Human Rights Watch World Report 2025
prison_adds.summary: thin: no usable finding — the HRW World Report 2025 Kyrgyzstan chapter contains no content on transgender prisoners or prison housing; its only prison references concern journalists and opposition activists sentenced to prison terms (media repressions, freedom of expression), not placement or conditions of trans detainees.

records.current_summary:
Cambodia is workable for trans visitors. Nothing is criminalised — the country has never criminalised same-sex activity or gender expression — and the government is formally cooperative: it accepted all 12 SOGIESC recommendations at its 2024 Universal Periodic Review, including legal gender recognition, and hosted the UN Independent Expert on SOGI in 2023. Phnom Penh and Siem Reap, the country's two main cities, have visible trans communities and tourist infrastructure accustomed to diverse visitors.

The risks are street-level and police-level rather than legal: a human-rights organisation documents "shocking" harassment and abuse of transgender women in urban centres, including a reported police practice of targeting trans women (extortion and abuse). There is no legal gender recognition yet, no anti-discrimination law covering gender identity, and no hate-crime statute.

For a visitor: low probability of legal trouble; moderate probability of harassment if visibly trans outside tourist areas; police are a risk factor, not a protection, for trans women especially.

prison_adds.title: CHRC says transgender rights are observed in prison
prison_adds.summary: Khmer Times (19 Feb 2025) reports Cambodian Human Rights Committee (CHRC) president Keo Remy, speaking at the handover of an ambulance to Correctional Centre 2 at Prey Sar prison in Phnom Penh, said Cambodia observes transgender prisoners' rights: transgender offenders who have undergone sex-change surgery are transferred from Correctional Centre 1 (the men's facility) to Correctional Centre 2 (the women's facility). The statement was made in praise of the centre, not as a published regulation, and no statute or formal policy text is cited; the article also flags that prison overcrowding has worsened because of gang-crackdown arrests. This is the only direct documentation of trans-prisoner placement practice for Cambodia found in two search rounds.
